purpose: Four original static 3D scene candidates for age-banded discussion of stopping, turning, pivoting and pace-change decisions. This staged pack is not added to the live experimental bank.
globalLimits: A static freeze cannot establish speed, edge technique, stopping or pivot quality, scanning behaviour, puck-control quality, success or learning transfer.
Question answers are either visible-scene observations or conditional coaching suggestions. A coach must calibrate age fit, wording and whether each reference is a useful starting point.

candidates.title: Pause before the turn
candidates.objective: Notice a visible space before choosing where to slow down or turn in a simple practice picture.
candidates.briefing: YOU have the puck. Navy2 is your teammate. Gold1 is an opponent. Find room before choosing where to turn. Navy attacks the right net. This picture shows positions, not skating speed.
cues: Space around the players is visible, but no movement is shown.

candidates.limits: Static 3D scene candidate for coach calibration. The freeze shows locations, puck ownership and stated context only. It does not assess speed, acceleration, edge technique, stopping quality, turning or pivot execution, scanning behaviour, puck control, success, safety or transfer to live ice. Position answers are discussion starting points; multiple clear spaces may be reasonable. Coaching answers are suggestions, not a certified tactical key.

questions.prompt: What is true about this freeze?
questions.explanation: YOU have the puck, while the other players are separate from YOU. The picture gives places to look; it does not show how anyone skates.

questions.prompt: Which two things can you see here?
questions.explanation: The nearby teammate, opponent and open ice are visible cues. A speed result cannot be read from one still picture.

questions.prompt: Put this looking routine in order.
questions.explanation: This is a simple suggested routine: notice the players, choose a visible pocket and then look again as the practice changes. It does not prescribe a measured skating technique.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to a different open practice spot with room from Navy2 and Gold1.
questions.explanation: This example leaves room from Navy2 and Gold1. Another clear spot may also work. Moving the marker does not show a turn.

questions.prompt: Navy2 stops in the space you chose. You want room for your turn. Where could you go?

options.text: The spot Navy2 is standing on

questions.explanation: Choose another clear space so you have room to turn. Being close to a teammate can sometimes help with a pass; here the task is to find room for your own turn.

questions.prompt: Tell the coach one space or player you would check before changing direction.
questions.explanation: Accept any child-specific observation that names Navy2, Gold1 or a visible open area. The response is a reflection, not a skating test.

metadata.teachingClaim: Young players can name nearby players and open ice before choosing a simple change of direction.
visibleEvidence: Space around the players is visible, but no movement is shown.
notAssessed: whether any choice succeeds on live ice
reviewQuestions: Is the pocket clear enough for a U7 child to point to?
Does the wording keep the focus on noticing rather than performing a stop or turn?
metadata.admissionLimit: Movement decision observation only. Does not close the skating-technique assessment gap.

candidates.title: Turn away from the wall
candidates.objective: Compare a wall-side location with a visible middle-space option before choosing a turn discussion.
candidates.briefing: YOU have the puck near the side boards. Navy2 is toward the middle. Gold1 is the nearest opponent. Compare the room by the boards with the room inside. Navy attacks the right net. Speed and stopping distance are not shown.
cues: YOU are close to the side boards.
Gold1 occupies the wall-side lane near YOU.
The middle of the rink has visible room between the marked players.

questions.prompt: Which player is closest to YOU in this picture?
questions.explanation: Gold1 is the nearest visible opponent to YOU along the wall-side area. Distance is a scene observation, not a prediction of who arrives first.

questions.prompt: Which visible cues could matter before a turn idea?
questions.explanation: The boards, Gold1 and the room toward the middle are all visible. Straight-line speed is not observable in a freeze.

questions.prompt: Arrange a suggested wall-side decision routine.

options.text: Notice the wall and nearby player

questions.explanation: The sequence keeps the child looking before and after choosing a space. It is a coaching prompt, not a required footwork order.

questions.prompt: Move YOU toward the middle to compare more room from Gold1.
questions.explanation: The example is farther from the side boards and Gold1. Check Navy2 and the next pressure cue; the position does not prove a safe turn.

questions.prompt: Gold2 moves into the middle space you planned to use. Which part of your plan needs another look?

options.text: The turn into that middle space
Where you started beside the wall
Who had the puck at the start

questions.explanation: Gold2 now occupies the space you planned to turn into. Reassess that route before committing. The starting position and starting puck owner have not changed; another route or a support pass could be useful if available.

questions.prompt: What did you notice near the wall before thinking about a turn?
questions.explanation: Accept a child-specific answer such as the boards, Gold1 or the available middle space. It is not evidence of edge control or turn quality.

candidates.title: Read space before a turn
candidates.objective: Read a visible pressure player and support space before discussing a pivot or continuation.
candidates.briefing: Navy attacks the right net. YOU have the puck but face back toward the left net. Gold1 is directly ahead of the way YOU face. Navy2 is on one side and Gold2 is on the other. Compare those spaces before deciding whether to turn. No movement is shown.
cues: Gold1 is directly in front of YOU relative to your facing.
Navy2 is visible in a separate support space toward the side boards.
Gold2 is not beside the puck carrier.

questions.prompt: Who is directly in front of YOU relative to the way YOU face?
questions.explanation: Gold1 is directly ahead of the way YOU face. Facing does not tell us skating speed or where anyone will move next.

questions.prompt: Which two cues help you compare a turn with keeping the puck here?
questions.explanation: Gold1 ahead, Navy2 in support and the separate Gold2 location are visible. A freeze cannot supply a speed number or prove an edge choice.

questions.prompt: Arrange a suggested pressure-and-support check.

options.text: Choose a pivot or continuation idea and recheck

questions.explanation: This routine names the decision inputs before a player chooses a movement idea. It does not prescribe a technical pivot sequence.

questions.prompt: Move YOU toward Navy2’s side to compare an angle away from Gold1.
questions.explanation: The example is closer to Navy2 and farther from Gold1. Recheck Gold2 and the passing route; neither a turn nor a completed pass is shown.

questions.prompt: Gold1 leaves the space ahead of YOU. Navy2 remains available for support. Which option has just become worth comparing with the support pass?

options.text: Holding the puck in the current spot
Carrying into the space Gold1 left

questions.explanation: Carrying into the newly available space is the changed option. Passing to Navy2 or holding briefly can still be defensible, depending on pressure and timing. Gold1 leaving alone does not prove that carrying will succeed.

questions.prompt: What visible relationship would you want to recheck before a pivot idea?
questions.explanation: Accept Gold1, Navy2, Gold2 or a described open-space relationship. The response is a coaching reflection, not a test of pivot execution.

candidates.title: Compare pressure and support
candidates.objective: Use defender distance, support and open ice as observations when discussing a pace change before a turn.
candidates.briefing: Navy attacks the right net. YOU have the puck and face back toward the left net. Gold1 is the nearest opponent ahead of the way YOU face. Navy2 is toward the nearby side boards; Navy3 is across the ice. Compare room to turn or change pace. No speed, acceleration or route outcome is shown.
cues: Gold1 is the nearest pressure player ahead of YOU.
Navy2 offers a visible support relationship toward the side boards.
Gold2 is across the play; Navy3 is separate from the puck carrier.

questions.prompt: Which observations could guide a pace-change discussion?
questions.explanation: The visible Gold1 relationship, Navy2 support and open spaces are useful observations. A still image cannot tell us YOUR exact speed or acceleration.

questions.prompt: Arrange a suggested pace-change decision routine.

options.text: Identify a space for a change of pace or turn

questions.explanation: The sequence emphasizes scanning and rechecking while choosing a movement idea. It does not claim that a particular pace or edge technique will beat Gold1.

questions.prompt: Move YOU toward Navy2’s side to compare the space between pressure and support.
questions.explanation: The example is closer to Navy2 but also slightly closer to Gold1. Compare that tradeoff and the pass lane; the marker does not demonstrate a change of pace.

questions.prompt: Gold2 moves into the direct line to Navy2. Which planned option needs to be reconsidered first?
questions.explanation: Gold2 now occupies the direct line to Navy2, so reassess that pass. Navy3 and carrying space are alternatives to compare, with Gold1 and the new pressure checked before committing. Neither alternative is guaranteed to work.

questions.prompt: Which two visible relationships would you compare before a pace-change idea?
questions.explanation: Accept any grounded pair such as Gold1 with Navy2, Gold1 with open ice, or Gold2 with Navy2. This records reasoning and does not assess speed or mechanics.
